sceneEn: A friend is asking you for a recipe from your home country. List the ingredients, then describe the steps in order and in the passive.
partnerEn: a curious friend who is just learning to cook
openingEn: You said you were cooking something from home. How is that actually made?
goalEn: The ingredients have been listed, the steps have been described in order and your friend could repeat the recipe.

sceneEn: You have come to an inn for two. You are being seated, talking to the waiter and ordering, and asking for the bill at the end.
partnerEn: a polite waiter who is rushed off their feet
openingEn: Good evening! Have you booked, or shall I show you to a table?
goalEn: You have been seated, food and drink have been ordered, the bill has been asked for and the tip has come up.

sceneEn: You are at a stall at the market. You compare two products, ask about the price and the freshness, then make your choice and have it weighed.
partnerEn: a jokey stallholder who praises their own goods
openingEn: All fresh today! What can I get you — the mushrooms, or the carrots?
goalEn: Two products have been compared, the price has been asked, the choice has been made with reasons and it has been weighed.

sceneEn: You are invited to dinner at a friend's home. First you ask what to bring, then at the table you praise the food and ask for a recipe.
partnerEn: a hospitable host who is proud of their table
openingEn: Lovely that you're here! Do sit down — how do you find the food?
goalEn: What to bring has been discussed, the table has been praised and a recipe has been asked for.

sceneEn: You are at a barbecue. You introduce the dish you brought and describe who made it and how it is made, with relative clauses.
partnerEn: a sociable neighbour who wants to taste everything
openingEn: That smells fantastic! What have you brought, then?
goalEn: The dish you brought has been introduced and who made it and how it was cooked have been described with relative clauses.

sceneEn: The wrong dish has come to your table at a restaurant and there is a mark on the plate. You say so politely, give your reason and ask for a solution.
partnerEn: a restaurateur who is defensive at first but then finds a solution
openingEn: Right, one schnitzel — enjoy your meal! Is everything all right for you?
goalEn: The wrong order has been raised, the reason has been given and a solution has been agreed.

sceneEn: A lot is left over after a big meal. You and your flatmate discuss what to keep and how, and what to do with what tomorrow.
partnerEn: an organised flatmate who cannot bear waste
openingEn: Well, that really is a lot left over. What are you going to do with it?
goalEn: A plan has been given for each of the leftovers and the two of you have agreed who does what.

sceneEn: You and a German friend are comparing table customs: what time people eat, what they drink, how a guest is treated. Describe the differences with paired conjunctions.
partnerEn: a curious friend who likes questioning their own customs
openingEn: Tell me, you eat a hot meal in the evening, don't you? With us it's quite different.
goalEn: At least three customs have been compared and the similarities and differences have been given with paired conjunctions.

sceneEn: There is a celebration at home and you have two hours left. You share out the work with a friend: who does what, and which job comes before which.
partnerEn: a friend who has come to help but does not know what to do
openingEn: I'm here! Just tell me what to do — what do we start with?
goalEn: The jobs have been put in order and it has been settled who does what and when.

sceneEn: You are at the end of a lovely meal and you have to go. You thank your host, offer to help, arrange the next meeting and say goodbye.
partnerEn: a warm host who does not want to let you go
openingEn: Is it that late already? Do stay a bit longer — there's coffee coming.
goalEn: Thanks have been given, help has been offered, the next meeting has been arranged and goodbyes have been said.

sceneEn: You have seen the same product in two places. You and a friend compare the prices, the discount and the quality and decide where to buy it.
partnerEn: a careful friend who never buys without comparing
openingEn: Have you compared the two prices? Which is cheaper?
goalEn: The two sellers have been compared on price and quality and a decision has been made with reasons.

sceneEn: You have gone back to the shop to exchange something you bought two weeks ago. You give your reason, show the receipt and say clearly what you want.
partnerEn: an assistant who sticks to the rules but looks for a solution
openingEn: Good afternoon! What can I do for you — would you like to exchange something?
goalEn: The reason for the return has been given, the receipt has been shown and an exchange or a refund has been agreed.

sceneEn: You have come to the bank to open an account. You find out about the fees, the card and the conditions for withdrawing money, with indirect questions.
partnerEn: an unhurried bank clerk who enjoys explaining
openingEn: Good afternoon! You'd like to open an account — have you any questions already?
goalEn: The type of account, the fees and how the card is used have been found out and the next step to open it has been agreed.

sceneEn: There is a problem with something you ordered online: the wrong model came and the manual is missing. You ring customer service and describe what happened in order.
partnerEn: a methodical agent who asks for the order number first
openingEn: Customer service, good afternoon! What is it about your order?
goalEn: What was ordered, what arrived and what is missing have been described and a solution has been agreed.

sceneEn: You are trying clothes on in a shop. You talk about the size, the fabric and the price, describing what you are after with adjectives in front of the noun.
partnerEn: a keen assistant who wants you to try everything on
openingEn: Can I help you? Are you looking for anything in particular?
goalEn: The item you wanted has been described with adjectives, tried on, and it has been decided whether to buy it.

sceneEn: You are in a hardware shop and you do not know the name of the part you want. You describe what it is made of, what it does and where it goes.
partnerEn: a patient shopkeeper who listens and tries to find the right part
openingEn: What are you looking for? Just describe it — what do you need it for?
goalEn: The part has been described by its material and its function and the shopkeeper has found the right one.

sceneEn: You and a colleague are discussing how your industry is going: production, competition, imports. Give both sides of each view with paired conjunctions.
partnerEn: a pessimistic colleague who is open to the figures
openingEn: Tell me, how do you see the state of our industry at the moment?
goalEn: A view has been given on at least three points, both sides of each have been said and a shared conclusion has been reached.

sceneEn: You are presenting last year's figures at a small meeting. You describe what the table shows, interpret one figure and answer the questions.
partnerEn: a team member who asks about the reason behind the figures
openingEn: Thanks for the table. What exactly is being shown there?
goalEn: The content of the table has been described, one figure has been interpreted and at least one question has been answered.

sceneEn: You and a friend are looking at a second-hand advertisement. You describe the advert, say what is good and what is doubtful about it, and list the missing details.
partnerEn: an optimistic friend who is ready to be taken in by the advert
openingEn: Look at this advert here — sounds great, doesn't it?
goalEn: The advert has been described, at least two missing details have been listed and the questions to ask the seller have been decided.

sceneEn: You are ringing an authority: the document you sent has been lost. You describe what you sent, what you are expecting and what you will put in a written complaint.
partnerEn: a polite official who avoids taking responsibility
openingEn: Administration office, good afternoon. How can I help you?
goalEn: The lost document has been described, your expectation has been put politely and an address for a written complaint has been taken.

sceneEn: You are looking for your train at the main station. You did not quite catch the announcement: you ask about the platform, the departure time and whether your ticket is valid for the return.
partnerEn: a helpful station attendant who is in a hurry
openingEn: Can I help you? You look as if you're looking for something.
goalEn: The platform, the departure time and what the ticket covers have been found out and the passenger has been sent to the right train.

sceneEn: Your flight has been delayed and you have missed your connection. At the airport desk you describe what happened in order and ask for a new solution.
partnerEn: an airline agent checking the system and looking for a solution
openingEn: Good afternoon! What's happened — which flight had you booked?
goalEn: What happened has been described in order and a new flight or a place to stay has been found.

sceneEn: You and a friend are setting off on a long drive. You talk about what you will do if things come up on the way: petrol, breaks, the weather.
partnerEn: a travelling companion who wants every eventuality talked through
openingEn: Six hours' driving — what do we do if we get tired?
goalEn: What to do has been settled with conditional clauses for at least three eventualities.

sceneEn: You are explaining the traffic rules here to a friend who has just arrived in the country: right of way, one-way streets, the pavement, parking. Give the rules impersonally.
partnerEn: a friend who has driven in another country and likes comparing
openingEn: It was quite different where I come from — what's actually forbidden here?
goalEn: At least three rules have been described impersonally and one difference between the two countries has been given.

sceneEn: You and a friend are comparing two places to stay on holiday: price, location, quiet. In the end you choose one.
partnerEn: a friend who watches the budget but will not give up comfort
openingEn: So, cabin or hotel? I really can't decide.
goalEn: The two options have been compared on at least three criteria and a decision has been made with reasons.
